title: Understand Area
goal: I can find area by covering a shape with unit squares, with no gaps and no overlaps, and counting them.
catchAll: Cover the inside with unit squares, no gaps and no overlaps. Then count every square once.

teacher.def: number of unit squares needed to cover the INSIDE of a shape or region
a square that is 1 unit tall and 1 unit wide

glossary.unit square: the square we tile with: each side is 1 unit long
glossary.square unit: a square that is 1 unit tall and 1 unit wide
glossary.tiling: covering a shape with unit squares, with no gaps and no overlaps
glossary.area: how much flat space is inside a shape

screens.title: What is area?
text: Area is how much flat space is inside a shape.
We find it by covering the inside with unit squares and counting them.
screens.caption: This rectangle is covered by 15 unit squares.

screens.title: A square unit
text: Your teacher's words: a square unit is "a square that is 1 unit tall and 1 unit wide".
We tile with these squares (unit squares), and we write area in square units.
screens.caption: One square unit

screens.title: Tiling: no gaps, no overlaps
text: Tiling means covering a shape with unit squares.
The squares must touch with no gaps, and none may lie on top of another.
A gap leaves space that is not counted. An overlap counts some space twice.
screens.caption: A correct tiling: every square touches its neighbors.

item.prompt: Which figure is tiled correctly to find its area?

options.why: Figure A has gaps between the squares. Some space is not covered.
In Figure C some squares lie on top of others, so space is counted twice.

item.yes: Yes! Figure B has no gaps and no overlaps.

screens.title: Explain My Thinking: no gaps, no overlaps

item.prompt: Why must unit squares cover a shape with no gaps and no overlaps? Write your answer in a sentence.
hints: Think about what happens to the count if a space is empty, or if two squares are on top of each other.
item.example: Unit squares must cover the shape with no gaps and no overlaps, so every part of the shape is counted exactly once.
show: Write one sentence that answers the question.
Here is one way to say it: Unit squares must cover the shape with no gaps and no overlaps, so every part of the shape is counted exactly once.

screens.title: Count the unit squares
text: Count each square once. Counting row by row helps you not skip any.
This rectangle has 2 rows of 6: 6 + 6 = 12. Its area is 12 square units.
screens.caption: 2 rows of 6 unit squares

screens.title: Inside, not the edge
text: Area is about the inside of a shape.
Walking around the edge of a rug is not area. Covering the rug is area.
screens.caption: The inside is what we cover.

item.prompt: What is the area of the shape in square units?
hints: Count the squares in each row, then add the rows.

watch.takeaway: Cover the inside with unit squares, no gaps and no overlaps, then count each square once. The count is the area in square units.

steps.say: Problem: what is the area of this rectangle?
Step 1: Check the tiling. The squares touch, with no gaps and no overlaps.
Step 3: Count the rows. There are 3 rows of 4.
Step 5: Name the unit. The area is 12 square units.

why.prompt: Why do we count row by row?

options.text: So we do not skip or count a square twice.
Because rows are bigger than columns.
options.why: Rows and columns hold the same squares. Counting in order just keeps track.
The order of counting does not change the area.

why.yes: Yes! Counting in order means every square is counted once.

examples.title: Example B: a tiling with gaps

steps.say: Problem: can we find the area from this tiling?
Step 1: Look between the squares. There are gaps.
Step 2: The gaps are inside the shape, but no square covers them. They would not be counted.
Step 3: Fix it: slide the squares together so they touch.
Step 5: The area is 15 square units.

why.prompt: What is wrong with a tiling that has gaps?

options.why: With gaps there are too few squares covering the inside.

options.text: Some of the inside is not covered, so it is not counted.
The squares are the wrong color.
options.why: Color does not matter. Covering the whole inside does.

why.yes: Yes! Every bit of the inside must be covered.

steps.say: Problem: only some tiles are drawn. What is the area?
Step 1: The top row has 5 tiles, so every row needs 5.
Step 2: The left side shows 3 rows.
Step 5: The area is 15 square units.

sections.heading: What your child is learning
sections.text: Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape. Your child covers a shape with unit squares (no gaps, no overlaps) and counts them. The count is the area in square units.

sections.heading: Try it with real things
list: Cover a placemat with sticky notes or square crackers. Count them.
Lay square tiles with a gap on purpose. Ask: what space is not counted?

sections.heading: Questions to ask
list: What does one unit square cover?
Are there any gaps or overlaps?
How did you make sure you counted each square once?

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Counting only the tiles that are drawn when part of the shape is empty.
Counting the squares along the edge only.
